data.title: Anthropic may get junk credit rating after its IPO, Blackstone says: report
data.description:
• Anthropic (ANT) may receive a high-yield, or junk, credit rating after its IPO, which can complicate the AI company's plans to borrow money to fund its growing infrastructure spending, according to a media report. 
  • Blackstone (BX), an anchor investor in Anthropic's $63B chip financing deal known as Project North Star, has told investors that the company is more likely to receive a rating in the double-B range or higher, according to the Financial Times report.
  • An investment-grade rating would allow Anthropic to borrow at lower costs to finance its artificial intelligence infrastructure projects.
  • Anthropic has more than $112B in cash and equivalents, while investors expect the company could raise about $100B through its IPO, the report said.

data.title: ‘Don’t rule out further drawdowns’ in tech as current cycle hits 22 drawdowns in only two years – Turning Point Market Research
data.description:
The technology sectors have already seen 22 drawdowns in performance since 2024, while the 1995-2000 tech bubble had 36 in total, according to Turning Point Market Research analysts.

Currently, the average public tech stock is down 37.1% from its 52-week high, due to the ongoing sell-off across AI stocks (AIQ), semiconductors (SMH), (XSD), and the overall technology sector (XLK), (VGT).

From 1995 to 2000, technology sub-industries experienced 36 independent drawdowns of 20% or more, compared with 22 since 2024, Turning Point Market Research analysts noted.

Within the technology sub-industries, internet services and infrastructure saw 10 drawdowns between 1995 and 2000, and only one from 2024 until now.

The biggest drawdowns in the past two years were in electronic components and semiconductors. Each sub-sector saw three.

The deepest drawdown in recent years in semiconductors (SMH), (XSD) was -35.1%.

 

 

 

“With that in mind, don't rule out further, potentially more painful drawdowns,” Turning Point analysts said. “Drawdowns are a common feature of major innovation cycles.”

data.title: Bispecific biotech Bambusa and Parkinson’s-focused Aspen slide on trading debuts
data.description:
Bambusa Therapeutics (BBTX), developer of bispecific antibody therapies, and Aspen Neuroscience (ASPE), a cell therapy developer focused on Parkinson’s disease, traded lower on Friday as their shares made listing debuts on Nasdaq.

Boston-based Bambusa started trading at $14.88 at about 11.00 am ET, implying roughly a 7% decline from its IPO price of $16.00 per share, which raised the company approximately $168.9M.  

On Thursday, the company upsized the offering to ~10.6M shares compared with its initial plans to sell 9.4M shares at $15-$17, which would have generated $150.4M in gross proceeds at the midpoint.

Bambusa (BBTX) expects to use net proceeds together with its existing cash resources primarily to advance its lead asset, BBT001, which is set to enter mid-stage development for Alzheimer's disease this year.

San Diego-based Aspen (ASPE), whose backers include Gilead Sciences (GILD), opened for trading at $14.70 at about 11:40 am ET before reaching $12.00 about an hour later to indicate roughly a 20% drop from the IPO price of $15.00.

On Thursday, the company priced the offering of ~9.4M shares at the low end of its marketed range, aiming to raise about $140.6M in gross proceeds, which it intends to use mainly to advance its lead product candidate, sasineprocel.

The one-time therapy is currently undergoing a Phase 1/2a trial for mid-stage to moderately advanced Parkinson’s disease, ahead of a late-stage trial initiation in H2 2027, subject to regulatory feedback.

data.title: FedEx Freight rallies on Q3 results and improved outlook for transition period
data.description:
Shares of FedEx Freight (FDXF) were launched higher Friday after reporting better-than-expected third-quarter results and raising its outlook for the transition period ending on December 31.

“While we are in the early stages of our journey as an independent company, we are encouraged by the momentum we are seeing across our operational, commercial, and technology initiatives. Guided by a clear and consistent strategy, we remain confident in the opportunities ahead and our ability to continue strengthening the business for long-term success,” FedEx Freight CEO John Smith said on Thursday.

For the four-month period ending September 30, revenue grew 9.2% as revenue per shipment increased 10.1% primarily by higher fuel surcharges, greater weight per shipment, and an increase in base revenue per hundredweight. Excluding fuel surcharges, revenue per shipment was up a much more modest 1.6%.

Higher costs to operate the standalone business, compensation and merit-related expenses, and expenses tied to separating FedEx Freight (FDXF) from FedEx (FDX) drove operating income down 6.1% to $383M. However, stripping out certain charges, adjusted operating income was up 16.4% to $510M, translating into a 90-basis-point expansion in the company’s operating margin to 15.5%. 

At the same time, unadjusted earnings declined by 43%, but increased 24.6% to $2.15 on an adjusted basis.

For the current 3-month quarter, FedEx Freight (FDXF) expects to earn an adjusted profit of $0.65 and $0.75 per share on $2.30B and $2.37B in sales. This compares to estimates of $0.54 and $2.23B, respectively.

For the 7-month transition period ending on December 31, revenue is expected to be between $5.58B and $5.65B, up from original guidance for an increase of 4% to 6%. This includes $2.3B and $2.37B in sales for the final three months of 2026 versus estimates of $2.23B.

Earnings for the transition period ending December 31 are expected to be between $2.80 and $2.90 per share, up from a prior forecast of $2.40 and $2.60 per share.

data.title: Quaker Houghton anticipates full-year adjusted EBITDA to rise a high single-digit % vs. 2025 amid continued raw material inflation
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Quaker Houghton (KWR) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "Our positive earnings momentum continued in the third quarter as we delivered our fifth consecutive quarter of year-over-year profitability growth... This resulted in the highest adjusted EBITDA in our company's history for the second consecutive quarter." (CEO, President & Director Joseph Berquist)
  • "Sales volumes increased 3%... and achieved net share gains in the mid-single digits... This represents our 12th consecutive quarter of positive net share gains." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • "Through the first three quarters, operating cash flow totaled $48 million, below recent periods primarily due to higher working capital... We are taking focused actions to improve cash conversion by unwinding the inventory we built to support our network transitions." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • "Actions taken during the year under this program will generate annualized run rate savings exceeding $10 million." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • "Immediately following the third quarter, we closed on the company's first ever term loan B... [which] provides greater financial flexibility... by extending our debt maturity profile and reducing required debt payments." (Executive VP, CFO & Principal Accounting Officer Tom Coler)

Outlook

  • "We expect to see normal seasonal demand patterns during the fourth quarter... While global fourth quarter volumes have declined by an average of 4% over the past five years sequentially from Q3... [there is] a possibility of a slightly more pronounced seasonal decline." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • "Based on our current outlook... we anticipate incremental raw material inflation in the fourth quarter and do not expect a significant decline in input costs until sometime in 2027." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • "We expect stable product margins in the fourth quarter, with targeted pricing actions tempering inflation... [and] we expect fourth quarter revenue and profitability to exceed the prior year, and full-year adjusted EBITDA to improve an estimated high single-digit percentage against 2025." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • Compared with last quarter’s tone on easing costs, management shifted from "expect... input costs... begin to moderate as we progress through the back half of the year" (CEO, President & Director Berquist, Q2) to "do not expect a significant decline in input costs until sometime in 2027" (CEO, President & Director Berquist, Q3).

Financial Results

  • "Third quarter net sales were $545 million, a 10% increase from the prior year... Gross margins... declined 130 basis points year-over-year to 35.5% due to product margin pressure from higher raw material costs." (Executive VP, CFO & Principal Accounting Officer Coler)
  • "We delivered $90 million of adjusted EBITDA in the third quarter, while adjusted EBITDA margin of 16.5% increased 50 basis points sequentially." (Executive VP, CFO & Principal Accounting Officer Coler)
  • "Our third quarter GAAP diluted earnings per share were $1.73, and our non-GAAP diluted earnings per share were $2.39." (Executive VP, CFO & Principal Accounting Officer Coler)
  • "Cash generated from operations was $14 million in the third quarter... driven by higher working capital outflows... [and] increased inventory associated with opening our new manufacturing facility in China and closing our facility in Dortmund, Germany." (Executive VP, CFO & Principal Accounting Officer Coler)

Q&A

  • Michael Harrison, Seaport Research Partners: asked whether EMEA margins are a new floor and could move higher; CEO Berquist: "I certainly hope that we've seen the floor... and that there is potentially more upside there," citing "closure of the plant in Germany," "decisions to exit... contracts" with weaker profitability, and "we're winning new business there and it's good business." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • Michael Harrison, Seaport Research Partners: asked if SG&A benefits were one-time and whether low-to-mid 20% of sales is sustainable; CEO Berquist: "There was nothing in the quarter that was unusual... we'd like to be in that low to mid-20s percentage for SG&A going forward." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • Michael Harrison, Seaport Research Partners: pressed on Q4 seasonality and pricing; CEO Berquist: "What I would expect this year is similar... somewhere in that 4% range," and "there will be some index adjustments in the fourth quarter" alongside "selective... targeted" pricing actions. (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • Jonathan Tanwanteng, CJS Securities: asked about customer restarts and whether they cannibalize other business; CEO Berquist: "I wouldn't say it's going to cannibalize anything at all," adding North America showed "relative strength" with metals up while "the automotive sector is down 2%." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • Jonathan Tanwanteng, CJS Securities: asked about gross margin trajectory beyond Q4; CEO Berquist: "we would expect to be above that 36% sustainably. But it may take us a quarter to get there"; CFO Coler: "fully expect as we move into 2027... margins into our target range of 36% to 37%." (CEO, President & Director Berquist; Executive VP, CFO & Principal Accounting Officer Coler)
  • Peter Osterland, Truist Securities: questioned pricing power in Asia amid China softness; CEO Berquist: "we do expect to get our margins at historical levels... [but] usually seen a lag of one to two quarters" and called Q3 inflation impact in Asia "more pronounced." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • Peter Osterland, Truist Securities: asked about 2027 supply security; CEO Berquist: "We are confident in our ability to continue to supply... reliably... not looking at anything that would cause us to say we'll have inability to supply... in 2027," while noting conditions are "very dynamic." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • Arun Viswanathan, RBC Capital Markets: asked for a 2027 volume framework by region; CEO Berquist: "we would expect in 2027 to have positive volume growth, positive revenue growth and positive EBITDA growth overall... we will grow our EBITDA in 2027." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)

Sentiment Analysis

  • "Just kind of wondering... is this maybe a new floor" and "do you expect that you can fully price through inflation without losing market share?" reflected slightly negative-to-skeptical analyst tone focused on margin durability, pricing power, and macro seasonality. (Michael Harrison, Seaport Research Partners; Peter Osterland, Truist Securities)
  • Management tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks ("Our positive earnings momentum continued") but more cautious in Q&A around inflation timing ("it may take us a quarter") and seasonality uncertainty ("possibility of a slightly more pronounced seasonal decline"). (CEO, President & Director Berquist; Executive VP, CFO & Principal Accounting Officer Coler)
  • Versus last quarter’s narrative that costs would "begin to moderate" in the back half (CEO, President & Director Berquist, Q2), the current quarter introduced more hesitant timing language ("do not expect a significant decline... until sometime in 2027"). (CEO, President & Director Berquist)

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Pricing/inflation narrative shifted from Q2’s "input costs... begin to moderate as we progress through the back half of the year" (CEO, President & Director Berquist, Q2) to Q3’s "do not expect a significant decline in input costs until sometime in 2027" (CEO, President & Director Berquist, Q3).
  • Execution emphasis broadened from Q2’s conflict-driven supply continuity ("maintain supply continuity") to Q3’s mix of share gains plus structural actions, including "term loan B" financing flexibility and cash conversion focus tied to China ramp and Germany closure. (CEO, President & Director Berquist; Executive VP, CFO & Principal Accounting Officer Coler)

Risks and Concerns

  • "Raw material costs remained elevated around the world... [and] we anticipate incremental raw material inflation in the fourth quarter" with relief dependent on conflict resolution. (CEO, President & Director Berquist)
  • Working-capital pressure and network transition risk remained prominent: "we temporarily increased inventory during the transition to our new production facility in China and the closure of our plant in Germany." (CEO, President & Director Berquist)

Final Takeaway

Management described Q3 as a continuation of profitability momentum, driven by share gains, pricing, and cost actions, while highlighting that inflation is persisting longer than previously framed. Leadership pointed to seasonality risk in Q4, an expectation for incremental raw material inflation, and a later timeline for input-cost relief, alongside targeted pricing, structural savings exceeding $10 million in annualized run-rate, and balance-sheet actions intended to preserve financial flexibility for continued growth initiatives and potential strategic M&A.

data.title: Vale rises after reporting mixed Q3 results, maintaining production guidance
data.description:
Vale (VALE) rose 2.3% in Friday's trading after reporting Q3 pro forma EBITDA of $3.51B, down 20% Y/Y and 14% Q/Q but above $3.32B expected by analysts surveyed by Bloomberg, and net operating revenues rose 2% Y/Y to $10.6B.

The Brazil-based miner said the decline in earnings reflected lower realized iron ore fines prices and external cost pressures, including Brazilian real appreciation and higher bunker prices.

Q3 iron ore production fell 6% Y/Y to 88.35M metric tons, below Bloomberg's 91.64M-ton average estimate, mainly reflecting lower availability at the critical Serra Norte mine, while setting a new quarterly record at Serra Sul and adding volumes from the Capanema and VGR1 projects.

Q3 iron ore sales edged up 0.3% despite the decline in production, while copper sales fell 4% and nickel sales jumped 16%.

Vale (VALE) maintained all FY 2026 production guidance, meeting at least the lower end of iron ore guidance of 335M-345M metric tons and the midpoint of the pellet production outlook of 30M-34M tons, while copper and nickel are expected in the upper half of their respective ranges of 360K-380K tons and 185K-200K tons.

data.title: Ondas stock drops despite expanded FEMA counter-drone funding
data.description:
Ondas (ONDS) shares fell 6.77% to ~$6.41 on Friday, despite the company outlining potential opportunities to supply counter-drone security systems to U.S. agencies under FEMA’s expanded $500M grant program.

The decline came as investors weighed potential share dilution and elevated short interest ahead of the company’s third-quarter earnings report. The stock found intraday support near ~$6.40, while its 14-day RSI fell to around 39, indicating weakening momentum.

The grant program includes an additional $250M in funding, extending eligibility to all 50 states, five territories, and the District of Columbia.

Ondas said its detection, tracking, and counter-drone systems could support public safety agencies as they expand security coverage across venues and critical infrastructure.

The company cited deployments at the 2026 FIFA World Cup and its selection to protect Jacksonville Jaguars NFL games as relevant experience.

It will also participate in a counter-drone security forum on November 9, 2026.

data.title: Global Payments surges on report CD&R pursuing takeover
data.description:
Global Payments (GPN) jumped 15% after a report that private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice is pursuing a take-private of the payments processor. 

CD&R has teamed up with private equity group GTCR, Global Payments’ biggest shareholder, on a joint bid for the company, according to a Financial Times report on Friday, which cited people familiar with the matter. Talks are ongoing, and a deal may not come to fruition.

Global Payments (GPN) has an enterprise value of about $40 billion.

data.title: Lear outlines $1.5B buyback through 2029 while scaling Orion automation with 10%-15% conversion cost reduction
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Lear Corporation (LEA) Q3 2026

Management View

  • “Sales increased 2% to $5.8 billion despite global industry production declining by 2% on a Lear-weighted basis.” (President, CEO & Director Raymond Scott)
  • “Adjusted earnings per share reached $3.71, a 33% increase from the third quarter of 2025, accelerated by our robust share repurchases this quarter.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)
  • “We generated operating cash flow of $329 million and free cash flow of $158 million in the quarter.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)
  • “We repurchased $175 million of shares in the third quarter, completing our full year repurchase target of $350 million.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)
  • “With our current authorization set to expire in 3 months, we increased our share repurchase authorization to $1.5 billion and extended it through 2029, reinforcing our commitment to returning capital to shareholders.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)
  • “Production in the state-of-the-art just-in-time seating facility begins next year… We expect automation to reduce the conversion cost requirements by 10% to 15%.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)
  • “After more than 34 years of dedicated service to Lear, Jason Cardew has elected to retire… Jared Fedele will succeed Jason as the CFO effective March 1.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)
  • “Core operating earnings were $256 million compared to $241 million last year, driven primarily by strong net operating performance.” (Senior VP & CFO Jason Cardew)

Outlook

  • “We have reduced our full year 2026 outlook for net sales… However… we are maintaining our full year outlook for core operating earnings.” (Vice President of Finance of Seating & E-Systems Jared Fedele)
  • “We increased our outlook for restructuring costs by $25 million… We adjusted our outlook for operating cash flow and free cash flow to support this investment.” (Vice President Fedele)
  • “In recent weeks, we have seen reductions in production schedules across several customers, particularly in China… we will continue to monitor the China domestic market, where consumer demand and production schedules continue to deteriorate.” (Vice President Fedele)
  • “We reduced our revenue midpoint by approximately $225 million, driven by lower production volumes on Lear programs, particularly in China, and the impact of foreign exchange.” (Vice President Fedele)

Financial Results

  • “Our sales increased 2% year-over-year to $5.8 billion… Adjusted earnings per share were $3.71 as compared to $2.79 a year ago.” (Senior VP & CFO Cardew)
  • “Third quarter operating cash flow was $329 million compared to $444 million last year due to higher tooling and engineering investments and the timing of working capital.” (Senior VP & CFO Cardew)
  • “Sales for the third quarter were $4.3 billion… Adjusted earnings were $274 million… with adjusted operating margins of 6.3%.” (Senior VP & CFO Cardew)
  • “Sales for the third quarter were $1.4 billion… Adjusted earnings were $69 million or 4.8% of sales compared to $60 million and 4.2% of sales in 2025.” (Senior VP & CFO Cardew)

Q&A

  • Dan Levy, Barclays Bank PLC: “There’s been a number of quarters now where you’ve underperformed… What’s going on in China? And how is this fixed?” Title Cardew: “A significant portion of our revenue in China… is in our nonconsolidated joint ventures… if you account for that, that business actually grew in the quarter.”
  • Dan Levy, Barclays Bank PLC: “Do you feel confident that… you can eventually return to more meaningful growth?” Title Cardew: “We see 2029, this business returning to significant growth above market… 3% to 4% in Seating and 4% to 6% in E-Systems.”
  • Dan Levy, Barclays Bank PLC: “Backlog… update?” Vice President Fedele: “Our 3-year core backlog is about $2.25 billion… Every program has been scrutinized to make sure it’s returning in excess of its cost of capital.”
  • Joseph Spak, UBS Investment Bank: “Where… within that range?” Title Cardew: “As we sit here today, our best estimate is right at the midpoint.”
  • Joseph Spak, UBS Investment Bank: “How… scale [Orion] across the enterprise?” (President, CEO & Director Scott): “I focus… around the brand-new plants… Some of them are very easy… Some of them are more… around… downtime to… make the capital adjustments.”
  • James Picariello, BNP Paribas: “Commodities… and… tariff reversal impacts?” Title Cardew: “The nonrecurring portion of the tariff revenue… is… $200 million or so… We have over $300 million in gross impact this year, and the net impact is only about $10 million.”
  • Rajat Gupta, JPMorgan: “Puts and takes in the 2027 margin bridge?” Title Cardew: “Wind-down… converting in the 20% range… Backlog typically is converting in the 10% range.”
  • Rajat Gupta, JPMorgan: “Available capital for return… into ’27?” Title Cardew: “We’re going to continue returning our excess cash to shareholders through share repurchases and dividends.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • “There’s been a number of quarters now where you’ve underperformed… What’s going on in China?” (Dan Levy, Barclays Bank PLC) reflected a skeptical tone centered on China mix, competitiveness, and timing of growth.
  • “As we sit here today, our best estimate is right at the midpoint.” (Senior VP & CFO Cardew) maintained a measured tone on Q4 variability, while management repeatedly emphasized execution and longer-dated inflection points.
  • In Q2, management said, “Our strong first half has given us confidence to raise full year guidance,” (President, CEO & Director Scott) while in Q3 management said, “We have reduced our full year 2026 outlook for net sales,” (Vice President Fedele) signaling a shift toward caution driven by China schedules.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Q2: “We have raised our full year guidance.” (President, CEO & Director Scott) vs. Q3: “We have reduced our full year 2026 outlook for net sales… [and] are maintaining our full year outlook for core operating earnings.” (Vice President Fedele)
  • Q2 highlighted the Rochester Hills integration center; Q3 elevated the Orion, Michigan JIT facility as the next-stage operating model: “This facility… reduces the conversion cost requirements by approximately 10% to 15%.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)
  • Q2 buyback commentary centered on an annual target (“raising our full year repurchase target to at least $350 million” (President, CEO & Director Scott)); Q3 shifted to longer-horizon authorization: “increased… to $1.5 billion… through 2029.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)
  • Q3 introduced a leadership transition not present in Q2: “Jared Fedele will succeed Jason as the CFO effective March 1.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)

Risks and Concerns

  • “Our current outlook assumes no changes to current tariff policies or significant industry-wide disruptions.” (Vice President Fedele)
  • “We have seen reductions in production schedules… particularly in China… consumer demand and production schedules continue to deteriorate.” (Vice President Fedele)
  • “We expect E-Systems to deliver positive net performance in the fourth quarter despite increasing copper and launch costs.” (President, CEO & Director Scott)

Final Takeaway

Management emphasized year-over-year earnings improvement and accelerated capital returns, while positioning Orion as the template for future seating productivity, stating the facility “begins next year” and is expected to “reduce the conversion cost requirements by approximately 10% to 15%.” Leadership framed the key near-term swing factor as China schedule softness—prompting a lower full-year sales view—while keeping profit expectations intact via restructuring actions, operational execution, and ongoing commercial negotiations, alongside a newly extended $1.5 billion share repurchase authorization through 2029.

data.title: AI is going to be something that changes economy - San Francisco Fed's Mary Daly
data.description:
Artificial Intelligence is going to be something that changes the economy, according to San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President and CEO Mary Daly.

Daly delivered introductory remarks before the San Francisco Fed's 2026 Economic Research Symposium on "AI and the Economy".

"It's going to be bigger than anything we've ever seen," said the San Francisco Fed president.

"This really matters for how we think about policy in the near and medium term. We have to know how technology affects growth, productivity, the labor market in the U.S. for us to think about our inflation, price stability, and full employment mandate," said Daly.

The way to do an analysis between promises and reality is to have evidence, she noted, adding that they are moving to a new center called the Technology and Growth Center.
